## What are meeting minutes?


Meeting minutes are the official written record of a meeting — not a word-for-word transcript, but a structured summary of what was discussed, what was decided, and who is responsible for next steps. Despite the name, they have nothing to do with the length of your meeting. Their purpose is to create a reliable reference that anyone can consult later, whether they attended or not.


Meeting minutes differ from personal notes in one key way: they're meant to be shared. That makes format and completeness more important than the rough jottings you'd keep for yourself.


## What to include in a meeting minutes template


Good minutes capture enough detail to be useful without burying the essentials in noise. At a minimum, every template should include:


- **Meeting title and type** — the name and purpose of the meeting (weekly team sync, board meeting, client kickoff, and so on)
- **Date, time, and location** — or the platform used for virtual meetings (Zoom, Microsoft Teams, Google Meet)
- **Attendees and absent members** — who was present and who was expected but missing
- **Agenda items** — the topics covered, in order
- **Decisions made** — what was agreed upon for each agenda item
- **Action items** — specific tasks with a named owner and due date for each
- **Next meeting details** — when and where the group meets next, if applicable


The more consistently you capture these fields, the more valuable your meeting record becomes over time.


## 6 meeting minutes templates for every meeting type


Not every meeting is the same, and your template should reflect that. Here's a comparison of the most common types, along with the sections that distinguish each one.


Meeting type Who uses it Key sections to include


General team meeting Any department Agenda items, decisions, action items, next meeting


Board meeting Executives, board members Quorum confirmation, motions, votes recorded


One-on-one Managers and direct reports Topics discussed, feedback, goals reviewed


Project kickoff Project teams Scope, roles, milestones, open risks


Weekly stand-up Agile and cross-functional teams Blockers, progress updates, sprint goals


Client meeting Account managers, sales Client requests, agreed deliverables, follow-up timeline


### General team meeting template


The most flexible format. Use it for recurring department syncs, all-hands updates, and ad hoc discussions that don't fit a more specific type.


**Key sections:** Meeting title, date and time, attendees, agenda items with brief discussion notes, decisions made, action items with owners and deadlines, next meeting date.


### Board meeting minutes template


Board minutes often carry legal weight, making them more formal than everyday notes. They should record whether a quorum was present, document votes taken, and note any formal motions moved or tabled.


**Key sections:** Organization name, meeting type, call-to-order time, attendees with titles, quorum confirmation, motions and vote counts, adjournment time.


### One-on-one meeting template


One-on-ones benefit from a running record. A consistent template helps managers and team members track feedback, goals, and progress over weeks and months.


**Key sections:** Employee and manager names, date, topics discussed, wins and challenges, goals reviewed or updated, agreed next steps.


### Project kickoff template


The kickoff meeting sets the tone for an entire project. Documenting scope, stakeholders, and open questions early helps everyone stay aligned when complexity increases later.


**Key sections:** Project name, date, attendees and roles, project scope and objectives, key milestones, identified risks, dependencies, next steps and owners.


### Weekly stand-up template


Stand-up notes are brief by design. Focus on blockers and progress rather than deep discussion summaries — the template should take minutes to fill out, not the full stand-up time.


**Key sections:** Date, team members present, blockers per person or team, updates since last stand-up, sprint goals for the week ahead.


### Client meeting template


Client-facing notes need to be clean and shareable. Focus on what the client asked for, what you committed to delivering, and when.


**Key sections:** Client name, internal attendees, client contacts, meeting purpose, topics discussed, client requests, agreed deliverables with due dates, follow-up contact.

## How to write effective meeting minutes


Having a template is a solid start. Using it well takes a bit of practice. These habits separate useful minutes from ones that end up ignored.


**Prepare before the meeting starts.** Review the agenda so you know what topics are coming. Set up your template in advance so you can fill it in as the discussion unfolds, not reconstruct it hours afterward.


**Record decisions and action items in real time.** Don't wait until after the meeting to write up what happened. Capture decisions as they're made and action items as they're assigned — including the owner and due date for each.


**Be concise and factual.** Your notes don't need to capture every word. Focus on decisions, commitments, and open questions. A tight summary is more useful than a verbose transcript.


**Send notes promptly.** The sooner you share minutes after a meeting ends, the more useful they are. Aim to send within 24 hours while context is still fresh.


**Use consistent formatting.** A shared template means anyone on your team can scan the notes quickly, regardless of who wrote them. That consistency matters more as your team grows.


## From manual templates to AI-powered notes


Manual templates are a solid foundation — but they still require someone to sit in the meeting and take notes, which means their attention is split between listening and documenting. AI note-taking shifts that dynamic. Instead of filling out a form by hand, AI captures what's said in real time, organizes the content automatically, and surfaces the decisions and action items you care about — so everyone can stay focused on the conversation rather than splitting attention between listening and taking notes.

## Frequently asked questions about meeting minutes templates


### **What are meeting minutes?**


Meeting minutes are the official written record of a meeting — a structured document capturing what was discussed, what was decided, and who owns the next steps. They're not a transcript of every word spoken. Their purpose is to give attendees and stakeholders a shared, reliable reference they can consult after the fact.


### **What's the difference between meeting minutes and meeting notes?**


Meeting minutes are formal, structured, and intended to be shared as the official record of a group discussion. Meeting notes are more informal — the personal jottings someone keeps for their own reference. Both have value, but minutes follow a consistent format and represent the meeting's outcomes for the whole team.


### **What are the most important elements of a meeting minutes template?**


Every meeting minutes template should include the date and time, the list of attendees, agenda items covered, decisions made, and action items with named owners and due dates. For formal meetings like board sessions, you'll also want to record quorum confirmation and any motions or votes taken.


### **How soon should meeting minutes be sent after a meeting?**


Most teams aim to distribute minutes within 24 hours. The sooner they go out, the more actionable they are — context fades quickly, and prompt distribution helps people start on their action items while the discussion is still fresh.


### **Can an AI tool like My Notes replace a meeting minutes template?**


For many teams, yes. My Notes automatically captures conversations in real time and organizes them into notes you can review, edit, and share — without a separate template. It works across Zoom, Microsoft Teams, Google Meet, and in-person meetings. If you prefer a manual starting point, a template and an AI note-taker can also work together: use the template as your structure and let AI fill in the details.


### **Is My Notes available for meetings outside of Zoom?**


Yes. My Notes works for Zoom meetings, Microsoft Teams sessions, Google Meet calls, and in-person conversations — all within the Zoom Workplace app. No separate bot or third-party integration is required for supported meetings.

For teams that want to go further, AI note-taking tools like My Notes take the manual work off the table entirely — automatically capturing, organizing, and helping you share notes from your Zoom meetings, Teams sessions, Google Meet calls, and in-person conversations.
